record.summary: Adam's Law, named after Adam Raine, sets child-safety duties for companion chatbot operators: age assurance using the device age-bracket signal, risk assessments before releasing a new or substantially modified chatbot, in-app crisis referrals and parental notice of credible self-harm risk, default settings only a parent can change, reasonable measures against self-harm, sexual, romantic-roleplay and manipulative outputs, an incident reporting mechanism overseen by the Attorney General, limits on targeted advertising, and independent compliance audits reported to the Attorney General. Families have a private right of redress.
record.notes: Known as Adam's Law. Passed the Senate 39-0 and the Assembly 64-4, with final legislative passage on 31 August 2026, and signed on 10 September 2026 as part of a 13-bill child online-safety package that also included SB 867 (companion chatbots in toys), AB 1709 (under-16 social media restrictions), AB 1856 (age verification signals) and SB 1276 (AI-generated child sexual abuse material). Authors: Senator Steve Padilla and Assemblymembers Buffy Wicks and Rebecca Bauer-Kahan. It builds on SB 243 of 2025 (US-CA-06), which required companion chatbot operators to disclose AI interaction and keep self-harm protocols, and on provisions of AB 1064 (Bauer-Kahan, 2025), and relies on the age-bracket signal of AB 1043 (Wicks, 2025).

verification.note: The Governor's release of 10 September 2026 (gov.ca.gov) confirms the signing of SB 1119, its title 'Companion chatbots: children's safety', its authors and the main protections of 'Adam's Law'. Senator Padilla's release of 31 August 2026 (sd18.senate.ca.gov) names Adam's Law as SB 1119, gives the floor votes and lists the bill's requirements as passed by the Legislature; the summary follows that list. The chaptered text, chapter number and operative date are not among the stored files. The status assumes California's default operative date for a statute without an urgency clause (1 January 2027); this needs checking against the bill text on leginfo.

legal_force.locator: Today's bills will help protect children by
legal_force.quote: “Adam’s Law” requires robust protections around companion chatbots for children, including crisis protocols in the case of suicidal ideation, parental controls, and notifications should a child disable safety settings.

summary.quote: Mandatory age assurance using the privacy protective age-bracket signal required pursuant to AB 1043 (Wicks, 2025).
Mandatory risk assessments before the release of a new or substantially modified companion chatbot.

Timely in-app crisis support requiring platforms to provide referrals to mental health resources, as well as provisions requiring notice to a parent if there is a credible threat of imminent of self-harm
Default settings that can only be changed by a parent, including no notifications, time limits on usage, and limitations on persistent conversational memory.

Liability for failure to take reasonable measures to prevent several categories of harmful outputs, including self-harm, sexually explicit material, romantic roleplaying, excessive praise or flattery, and emotionally manipulative outputs
Requirement to implement an incident reporting mechanism, overseen by the Attorney General.
Strict limitations on targeted advertising to children in conversational chats.
Mandatory independent audits of operator compliance, with findings submitted to the California Attorney General.
A private right of redress for families harmed by violations relating to crisis referral services, parental notice, default protections, and prohibitions on harmful outputs.

notes.quote: Adam’s Law builds on last year's SB 243, authored by Senator Padilla, which required chatbot operators to disclose that users are interacting with AI and to maintain protocols for detecting self-harm content.

judgment.status_reasoning: No change. The Legislature passed SB 1119 on Monday 31 August 2026 and the Governor signed it on 10 September 2026. Neither stored release gives an operative date or mentions an urgency clause. California statutes without an urgency clause become operative on 1 January of the year after enactment unless they say otherwise, which would be 1 January 2027, after today (14 October 2026); so 'Adopted, not yet in force' stays, with date_in_force left null until the chaptered text confirms the date.
judgment.scope_reasoning: Clearly in scope: an AI-specific state law regulating companion chatbots for child safety.
